newsitem.title: ITALY: Bossi camp sees separatism in N.Italy succeeding.
newsitem.headline: Bossi camp sees separatism in N.Italy succeeding.

text.p: Northern League leader Umberto Bossi's call for a breakaway state in northern Italy has fallen largely on deaf ears but supporters say his separatist message needs only time to succeed.
Delegates at a three-day party congress ending on Sunday voted by a wide majority to accept that the League should shun alliances with other political parties in forthcoming local elections.
"We have to sit down at a table to negotiate a share-out between the North and the rest of the country of the national wealth and the national debt," Enzo Erminio Boso, a League senator told Reuters.
Boso said he gave little credit to recent opinion polls showing scant support for the creation of a self-styled northern breakway state called Padania.
"Over the past six years the League has repeatedly been given up for dead," Boso said. "How can anyone be expected to believe the opinion polls of the state-controlled media?"
He added that he believed a referendum which the League is organising in April to poll support for an independent Padania would win strong backing.

But his optimism did not appear to be entirely shared by Bossi, who acknowledged in a speech to the party faithful on Saturday that conditions might not yet be ripe for the north to cut loose from the rest of the country.
"If secession arrives in a society which is not yet mature it ends up badly," Bossi said, although he has shown no sign of wanting to abandon his separatist agenda.
"Italy is finished. We have to get out of here. Let us leave," he added, speaking in front of a poster depicting a missile called "Free Padania" rising out of a swamp.

Calls by Bossi and other League leaders for an independent state brought an immediate rejoinder on Saturday from Prime Minister Romano Prodi who said the cause of separatism could prosper if Italy failed to join a single European currency.
"The League today is a movement which has one sole objective -- that of breaking Italy in two," Prodi told a conference in Rome.

"Our response will be entry into Europe (European economic and monetary union) and the start of a federalist reform which gets underway a measured and strong decentralisation. If we stay out of Europe, the League cashes in," Prodi said.

Prodi hopes membership in a European Union single currency and sweeping institutional reform can undercut support for the League, which rose to prominence on public disgust with political corruption and a crushing tax burden.
The League won more than 10 percent of the national vote in a general election last April on a federalist platform fashioned to appeal to Italians in the affluent north.
Bossi abruptly changed tack after the election, which gave the League its highest number of votes but failed to give him a pivotal role in politics.
He ditched federalism and espoused a separatist creed, but a declaration of independence for Padania fell flat last September, suggesting he had completely misread the popular mood.
An opinion poll published by the Milan newspaper Corriere della Sera suggested that northern Italians had not warmed to Bossi's new separatist programme.
The poll said 79.7 percent of 600 people questioned in northern Italy shared President Oscar Luigi Scalfaro's view that Italy was "single and indivisible".
